title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. We present the sealed design, execution accounting, contamination‑check evidence (10% Mininet holdout → 20 tasks; zero disagreements), representative examples, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating natural‑language intent→configuration translation with generative language models offers operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause service outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes combining LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) so unsafe candidates can be detected and corrected before application. The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by a chosen generator/prompt policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness.

Research question. We preregistered and asked a focused confirmatory question: Does an automated GVR pipeline that uses a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?

Contributions. (1) A sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) enforcing shared‑initial generation to isolate the effect of applying deterministic validation+repair to the same generated candidate. (2) A fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0). (3) A frank, artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome and interpretation that clarifies when automated repair can and cannot reduce validator‑detected failures, plus reproducibility notes and operational recommendations grounded in the archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: LLMs produce factual errors and are prompt‑sensitive; mitigation approaches include grounding (retrieval), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures [https://openalex.org/W4399803256; https://openalex.org/W4410125989]. Prototype NetOps systems show feasibility of intent→configuration synthesis but often lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies [https://openalex.org/W4399629579; https://openalex.org/W4403635865]. Architectures combining LLM generation with deterministic validators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers) and repair loops have been proposed to improve safety; empirical red‑teams and configuration‑brittleness studies warn that tool‑description injection and tool‑chaining can materially change safety outcomes [10.2139/ssrn.7203631; 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10646209/v1]. Surveys and prototype evaluations motivate externally auditable, preregistered measurements that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model and prompt policy [https://openalex.org/W4411523078]. Our study situates itself in this space by measuring a preregistered paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study preregistration (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02; preregistration SHA‑256: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6) specified a paired binary design with n = 200 tasks and a single pre‑registered primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided (α = 0.05). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confidence intervals used a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈ 30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; stopping rules and a model‑call cap (400) were frozen before execution.

Task bank and validators. The confirmatory sample comprised a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial/expected final states and explicit workflow constraints (e.g., make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields) and a required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces the encoded constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the execution produced a contamination summary artifact reporting zero disagreements.

Model configuration and shared‑initial semantics. The run used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini, provider label openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single deterministic initial candidate (temperature=0 sampling policy per preregistration) was produced and reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This isolates the effect of adding validator+repair on a fixed generator output and removes per‑condition sampling variance. Adapter accounting confirms hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}.

Repair policy, budgets, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task when deterministic_netops_validator_v5 reported violations (up to 200 repair calls allowed). The contamination_plan deterministically excluded tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagreed from the primary analysis; sensitivity analyses (pre‑specified) are included in the plan but not invoked because no disagreements occurred. Missingness and exclusion rules were fixed in advance and applied deterministically.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); zero repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Provider accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0.

Descriptive outcomes. analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity and contamination checks. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed and analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero validator–emulator disagreements. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts record pair_accounting_consistent = true and episode_accounting_consistent = true.

Representative diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (pair‑000001 … pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that matched task required_sequences and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 for each. Difficulty annotations in validator traces (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) confirm that tasks exercised medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints despite validator‑satisfying outputs.

Planned but uninvoked analyses. Secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are unpopulated because no repairs occurred; preregistered sensitivity branches for contamination handling were not invoked because no flags were raised.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate confirmatory outcome (zero baseline failures) demonstrates a logical operational point: when a chosen model, prompt policy, and sampling regime produce validator‑passing candidates for every item in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. The result therefore does not show that GVR is universally useless; it shows GVR’s marginal benefit is conditional on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage.

Why baseline failures were zero. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) the prompt template and deterministic shared_initial sampling policy produced candidates that conformed to explicit task‑bank constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes clear required_sequences that map directly to validator checks and hence may be easier for deterministic prompts to satisfy; (3) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces the task‑encoded intent constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic failure modes only visible under end‑to‑end device execution; (4) the single repair budget combined with shared_initial design removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a pathway for generating alternative, repairable candidates.

Operational implications. Before investing in automated repair pipelines, practitioners should (a) measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workload distributions, (b) evaluate validator coverage with end‑to‑end emulation or real devices, and (c) consider investments that increase validator fidelity, diversify generation (multi‑sample or multi‑model), or incorporate human‑in‑the‑loop approval. When baseline validator failures are non‑negligible, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains depend on repair budget, repair prompt engineering, and validator completeness.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded). Internal validity: preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and frozen stopping rules protect against post‑hoc design changes; however, shared_initial design trades generality for control and specifically removes per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 checks task‑encoded constraints but can miss device‑level or vendor‑specific behaviors only observable under end‑to‑end execution. External validity: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), one sampling policy (shared_initial deterministic), and a curated task bank were used; outcomes may differ across model families, nonzero temperature sampling, multi‑sample generation, larger repair budgets, or adversarial distributions. Conclusion validity: exact McNemar is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; nonetheless reporting the zero‑discordance outcome is a meaningful empirical datum for future workload selection and power planning.

Reproducibility note. All model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, and bootstrap parameters are archived in the execution bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/* artifacts). The Mininet holdout was executed and contamination summary reports no disagreements, but the randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact; this missing labeled seed prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of which 20 tasks were used for the emulator holdout despite the contamination_summary.csv evidence of zero disagreements. We disclose this reproducibility gap explicitly.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. The result highlights that automated repair’s marginal value is workload dependent: when baseline validator failures are rare, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity via richer emulation or devices, explore multi‑sample/multi‑model generation, and study multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 (preregistration SHA‑256: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6). Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) as required by the track; that immutable archived reference identifies the initial master prompt used but the prompt text is not reproduced here. Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks/tools: code and experiment orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: estimand, sample size (n = 200), paired design, stopping rules, model‑call cap (max = 400), repair call budget (≤1 per task), and shared‑initial generation semantics were frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle (representative artifact paths and hashes are recorded in the manifest). Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the labeled randomized seed used to select the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
